title: The Ratio Ceiling: Why a Full Waitlist Doesn't Mean a Fully Earning Childcare Centre
excerpt: Childcare centres across the East Coast are taking enrolments for 2027 with waitlists stretching months. Educator supply, not demand, is what is actually capping revenue.
content:
Term 4 is when most childcare centres across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria lock in enrolments for the year ahead, and this spring the waitlists at many centres run well past anything a single 2027 intake could absorb. For a business built on occupancy, a full waitlist should be the clearest possible sign of health. On its own, it rarely tells the director what she actually needs to know.

The constraint behind most childcare centres' revenue ceiling right now is not demand. It is the educator roster. A room licensed for a set number of children under two, or a set number of three to five year olds, can carry every one of those places as a confirmed enrolment and still run under its licensed number on a given day, because there are not enough qualified educators rostered against the ratio that room requires. The enrolment list and the billable place are two different things. The gap between them is where a meaningful share of expected revenue quietly goes missing, and it rarely shows up as a single clear number on a monthly report.

This is not a story about any particular centre getting something wrong. It is the pattern the whole sector is working through at the same time, shaped by a tight educator labour market rather than any one business's planning. The directors tracking it properly are making noticeably different staffing and pricing decisions to the ones still reading their occupancy straight off the enrolment list.

Licensed Capacity and Staffed Capacity Are Not the Same Number

Every room in an Australian childcare centre operates under a maximum ratio of educators to children, set under the National Quality Framework and varying by age band. Most directors know that ceiling without needing to look it up. Fewer track the number underneath it with the same discipline: how many qualified, rostered educators are actually available on an ordinary Tuesday once annual leave, parental leave, sick leave and the realities of current recruitment are accounted for. When that second number falls short of what the ratio requires for a fully enrolled room, the room's real capacity for the day is set by who turned up to work, not by the lease, the licence, or how many names sit on the waitlist. A business can be commercially full and operationally short in the same week, and the two numbers rarely get compared side by side.

The Educator Market, Not the Enrolment Pipeline, Is the Real Ceiling

Recruitment and retention pressure in early childhood education has been building for several years, and it shows up less as a single crisis and more as a steady, recurring cost of doing business. Vacancies sit open longer than they used to. Casual and agency educators fill gaps at a materially higher cost per hour than a permanent team member, and that cost attaches directly to the places those shifts are covering, not spread evenly across the roll. Many centres respond by quietly capping enrolment in a room below its licensed number rather than risk a ratio breach, which is the right compliance decision and a real revenue decision at the same time. That trade-off protects the centre's registration. It also means a director can be doing everything correctly from a child safety and compliance standpoint while the business absorbs a staffing-driven revenue gap that never gets named as its own line item.

What the Gap Costs, and How to See It Before Next Year's Enrolments Lock In

Fixed costs do not shrink when a room runs under its licensed number. Rent, compliance overheads, insurance and most of the administrative cost base are set at the centre's full licensed capacity regardless of how many of those places are actually staffed and billing on a given day. A centre quietly running below its licensed number while its cost base assumes something close to full is carrying a materially different margin story than its occupancy report suggests, and that gap compounds across every week it goes unmeasured. A Workforce Capacity and Utilisation Review is built for exactly this question: it separates licensed, enrolled and actually staffed place days into one view and attaches a dollar figure to the difference, so a director knows whether the constraint sitting underneath this year's waitlist is recruitment timing, roster design, or something the fee schedule needs to absorb rather than staffing alone.

For centres currently taking 2027 enrolments on the strength of a waitlist that looks reassuring on paper, the more useful number to check first is not how many families are waiting. It is how many of the rooms they are waiting for can actually be staffed against ratio on an ordinary week, and what that means for cash through the quieter months a cash flow discipline habit would otherwise catch early. faqs.q: Why does my childcare centre have a long waitlist but still miss its revenue targets?
faqs.a: A waitlist measures demand, not billable capacity. Revenue depends on how many of those places can actually be staffed against the required educator ratio on a normal day, after leave, turnover and recruitment timing are accounted for. When the roster falls short of what a fully enrolled room needs, that room runs under its licensed number regardless of how many families are waiting, and the gap between enrolment and staffed capacity is where expected revenue quietly disappears.

faqs.q: What staff-to-child ratios apply to childcare centres in Australia?
faqs.a: Ratios are set under the National Quality Framework and vary by the age of the children in each room, with younger age bands requiring more educators per child than older ones. The ratio is a hard ceiling a centre cannot cross, which means the number of qualified educators rostered on a given day, not the enrolment list or the licence, ultimately decides how many children that room can actually have in care.

faqs.q: How does the educator shortage affect childcare centre profitability?
faqs.a: Recruitment pressure raises the cost of every shift that has to be covered by casual or agency staff, while fixed costs like rent and compliance overheads stay the same whether a room runs full or under its licensed number. The result is a margin that compresses quietly rather than all at once. A Workforce Capacity and Utilisation Review measures exactly where that compression is happening across the roll.

faqs.q: What is the difference between licensed capacity and staffed capacity in childcare?
faqs.a: Licensed capacity is the maximum number of children a room is approved to hold under its registration. Staffed capacity is how many of those places can actually operate on a given day once the required educator ratio is met by rostered, qualified staff. A centre can be fully enrolled against its licence and still be commercially short if staffed capacity falls below it.

faqs.q: Can a childcare centre raise fees to cover rising staffing and recruitment costs?
faqs.a: Fee increases are one lever, but they only address part of the problem if the underlying constraint is staffing rather than price. Reviewing the fee schedule against current recruitment and casual staffing costs is worth doing annually, ideally alongside a clear view of staffed versus licensed capacity, so the fee change solves the actual gap rather than masking a rostering shortfall with a higher price.

faqs.q: How can a fractional CFO help a childcare centre manage staffing-driven revenue gaps?
faqs.a: A fractional CFO brings the recurring discipline of tracking licensed, enrolled and staffed capacity side by side, translating the gap into a dollar figure the director can act on each month. This sits above the compliance and payroll work a bookkeeper or accountant already handles well, adding the commercial lens that turns a staffing shortfall into a decision about recruitment timing, room design or pricing.

faqs.q: When should a childcare centre review its enrolment and staffing model each year?
faqs.a: Term 4, when most centres are locking in enrolments for the following year, is the natural point to review staffed capacity against the licence and the waitlist. Doing this before enrolment offers go out means recruitment gaps are identified while there is still time to act on them, rather than discovered mid-year when a room is already short.
